sired the Department of Justice to take action, it seems to me that the Department of Justice should have keen notified at the time of this theft. I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett) that so far as my knowledge goes, the matter has never been brought under the notice of the Department of Justice.

I understand it is contemplated by this amendment to do away with the necessity of using the stamp. Personally, I am opposed to that. The stamp was a safeguard to some extent against improper ballots getting out, and I do not think that the proposal of the Solicitor General to have the stubs numbered as well as the counterfoils, will be effective to prevent wrong-doing in this respect. We know from what took place in elections in the past, that the deputy returning officer was in league with those who did the dishonest work outside, and therefore the numbering of the ballots would not prevent fraud. If the number on the stub has to correspond with the number on the counterfoil, a dishonest deputy returning officer could hurry the ballot into the box without allowing the scrutineers to see it, or perhaps the scrutineers would not think it was their business to take the trouble to look at it. If the official stamp is used, it could readily be seen by all parties, and while the stamp is not an absolute guarantee of honesty,
I believe it provides some safeguard.

Wihat was it that Influenced the government to depart from that principle which they adopted in reference to accepting the provincial franchises for the Dominion elections ? Why did the Solicitor General make an exception of the North-west Territories ? When the Election Act was originally introduced, the Solicitor General did provide for the ordinance of the North-west Territories to be accepted, just as the franchises for the different provinces were accepted. This was sent to the Senate and was amended, making an exception for the Territories. That Bill was sent back to the Senate, and it was returned the second time and accepted by the House of Commons, it being the latter end of the session. What possible reason had the present government for departing from that principle when, as they claim, they were adopting the franchises of the different provinces ? Why make an exception of the Territories ?
The Territories have always had a special ordinance with respect to Dominion elections, and we have allowed that to continue. That is all.

You did not
accept the Territorial Representation Act.
No.
Why not ?
We allowed the Act to remain in force as heretofore. We saw no reason to make a change.
The Solicitor General withdrew at its second reading that portion of his Bill which referred to the North-west Territories, leaving it as it is now.
That was the objectionable part last year when we introduced the Bill.
Did not the Solicitor General himself favour that
I *do not remember what I favoured last session; that was previous to the election.

I am astonished to hear that the Solicitor General places the stealing of this ballot box on the same footing as the loss of a barrel of flour from a freight train. Here we had in that polling division the ballots of two hundred freemen of the Dominion of Canada, and that ballot box was stolen. The whole matter is in charge of the government of Canada. Not only the returning officer and the deputy returning officer, but the railway officials, are all under the control of the government of Canada, and between Alberton and Summer-side, one box was found to be stolen when the ballots were called on for a recount. There was a majority of thirty-three for me in that ballot box. The miscreant, the wretch who stole that box, knew well that if the judge would take a partisan view of it, and not having these ballots before him, that I would be counted out, and would not be here to-day to represent the people of West Prince. The Solicitor General places the stealing of that ballot box in which you had the rights, the franchises of two hundred freemen of the Dominion, on the same level as the loss of a barrel of flour on the railway. The railway officials would compensate for the loss of a barrel of flour or a cask of sugar or of molasses. But how are they going to repay the honest freemen of Canada for the loss of two 'hundred sacred votes. Sir, they have not sufficient money in the treasury of Canada, with all their surpluses, to repay the people for that Joss.
I ask the government; I ask the Solicitor General, representing in this House the Department of Justice, what action has he taken ? Nothing has been done to bring this thief to justice. No reward has been offered. The ballot box has been stolen, the ballots have been taken away, and these men were supposed to have been deprived of their rights and liberties as British freemen. When we are passing legislation of this kind, I ask the government to put a stop to that machine that is working all over Canada. It is a part of the machine that was working In the province of Prince Edward Island. I had occasion a few days ago to bring to the attention of the House

the fact that a man from La Patrie office was down working in Prince Edward Island for a few months prior to the last election. That man was on the train that evening watching everything when the ballot hox was stolen, and I solemnly and sincerely believe that that individual, being part of the machine that is working from the Atlantic to the Pacific, stole the ballot box, with the intention of depriving me of my seat and electing a supporter of this government. We only ask for justice and fair-play at the hands of the government, and that where a man honestly records his vote, that vote shall be counted in favour of the candidate for whom it is cast.

I have a Bill before the House to make certain amendments to the Election Act, particularly as regards the North-west Territories ; and if the Solicitor General will look at that Bill between now and the next time his Bill is taken up, and will adopt some of the amendments there proposed, he will save me the trouble of going on with it. It deals with certain grievances growing out of the late election which ought to be remedied.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock. DOMINION LANDS ACT AMENDMENT.
Bill (No. 29) to amend the Dominion Lands Act (Hon. Mr. Sifton), read the second time, and considered in committee.

I will explain briefly to the committee the different sections of the Bill. The first clause is for the purpose of enabling the minister to appoint an officer of the department to take the place of the Commissioner of Dominion Lands and sign documents in the absence of the commissioner. It has been customary for a number of years, when the commissioner has been away, for one of the other officers of the department to act in his place ; but a legal firm in a certain case has thrown a doubt upon the power of another officer to do so in the absence of a statutory provision, and I desire to put the question beyond a doubt by the amendment. The second clause is for the purpose of making the following change. At present, when a person makes a homestead entry, he is required by the Act within six months to prove the entry, otherwise it is void. As a matter of practice. it has never been customary to insist on that provision, and in order to bring the uniform practice of the department into accord with the law. I desire to have this clause amended so that the entry will not be void unless it is so declared by the minister. As to tlie third clause, I intend to ask to have the first two paragraphs struck out. The third paragraph has this effect. Two or three years ago a Bill was introduced by tlie then member for Western Assiniboia, providing that under certain circumstances the having of stock and corresponding improvements on a homestead should entitle a homesteader to a patent, in place of the usual cultivation conditions. This was to meet the case of persons who devoted themselves to raising stock instead of grain. The Bill of the hon. gentleman, which I accepted, required that one acre should be cultivated. That has been found to be of no value and vexatious, because in some cases the homesteader has been entitled in every other respect to a patent. Therefore, as a matter of convenience, I think it well to strike that out. Section 4 I will ask to have struck out as being unnecessary. Section 5 refers to a set of provisions in the Dominion Lands Act under which companies were authorized some years ago to make advances to settlers and to take liens on their homesteads. The plan did not prove to be a success, and has been more or less a source of embarrassment ever since. The majority of the settlers who came in under that plan did not turn out to be successful. But we have had to administer these clauses of the Act, and there were cases in which it was necessary to issue the patents to the companies which advanced the money. Some cases occurred in which there was no statutory provision for the issue of the patent, because the settler in whose name it had to be issued was not a British subject. Of course, under the ordinary law the patent cannot be issued unless the applicant is a British subject ; but when he has fulfilled the conditions, made his application and then left the country without liquidating the claim of the company which advanced money to him, and without taking out naturalization papers, the only way to enable the company to realize upon their security is to take authority to issue the patent without requiring the patentee to become a British subject. I would ask that section 6 be struck out. The effect of section 7 is to enable the minister to execute leases of Dominion lands when authorized by the regulations, without having to execute these leases under the great seal. That is simply a matter of departmental convenience and there is no object to be served in execut* ing the leases under the great seal. Section 8 is for the purpose of enabling all persons owing money to the Crown for or on account of Dominion lands to secure the benefit of the reduction in interest from 6 to 5 per cent, which was made under the Act of last session.
speakername: The MINISTER OP THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext:
Is there at present any commissioner of Dominion lands, or is this entirely a new function ?
2815	COMMONS	2816
The MINISTER OF THE INTERj.uK. The office of commissioner of Dominion lands has been a statutory office for ten or twelve years. It has been customary for another officer to sign the name of the'commissioner in his absence. I am not at all sure that this is not authorized by the Act, but a legal firm has raised the question, and I ask to have it made clear.
On section 2,

Under the present Act if a homestead entrj is not perfected within six months, it be: comes void. We have many applications for extensions of time, and this is to relieve the department of considerable work caused by these applications, by providing that the entries shall not become void by the mere lapse of time alone but that alter the six months have elapsed the minister must declare the entries void before the lapse oi' time takes effect.

I notice a good deal of work is thrown on the department by applications to have the time extended. I have sent in a number myself, but the question is whether this amendment would not leal to a greater abuse in another direction, by allowing people to hold lands indefinitely.
I do not see any provision for giving notice to the homesteader before the minister declares his entry void.
The power of the minister to declare it void only comes after the expiration of the six months, so that the homesteader has still as much time as he has now.
But still he will have no notice.

In every case thirty days notice is given before any action is taken affecting the entry. What the hon. member for East Grey said is perfectly true with regard to the early development of the North-west when many people went in and took up lands solely for speculation, but that practice has gone out of existence altogether, and the officers of the department are satisfied that this change will facilitate the administration of the Act.

Would not this tend to revive the system ? Trouble like this arose : A man went from Ontario intending to settle in that country and took up land, but afterwards returned to Ontario, and, owing to business affairs or some other cause, was unable to go back.' He found some person going into the country and sold his claim for a consideration. In the meantime, some one had applied for the cancellation of his title, and the party who had paid the consideration found some one else on the land.
that he was badly used, and the man who got it thought he was entitled to it.
The party who bought it had no right to buy it.

No legal right, but there seemed to be some sort of a moral right, since the original claimant's right had not been cancelled. I fear that this will revive the same system-not to the same extent, but to some extent at least.

I did not explain the latter part of this clause. The third subsection of section 36 of the Dominion Lands Act says :
Provided further, that in the case of immigrants from elsewhere than the North American continent the Governor in Council may extend the time for the perfecting of entry to twelve months from the date thereof.
It has been found unsatisfactory to confine that to immigrants from elsewhere than the North American continent. We are receiving a large number of settlers from the United States, and it is sometimes desirable thait they should, be brought within the same category. So, it is proposed to make the clause read thus :
3. Provided further, that in the case of any immigrant the time for perfecting his entry may be extended by the minister for any period not exceeding one year from the date upon which he obtained such entry.
I doubt if this is absolutely necessary, in view of the amendment made in the former provision, but it will make it clear.
I notice that you substitute 'minister ' for ' Governor in Council.' Why is that ?

It is absolutely useless ito have this go ito the Governor in Council, and it has ithe 'disadvantage of hanging up the departmental business. It is impossible for the Governor in Council to consider such applications as that. As a matter of fact, in the administration of the Dominion Lands Act, one of the greatest sources of embarrassment is the number of cases that have to go to the Governor in Council. The Act that we are amending has reference to the protection of game in the unorganized portion of the North-west Territories, the far northern part which is not organized, or represented in the North-west Territories Legislative Assembly. The section as it is in the original Act is as follows :
Any beast, bird or eggs in respect of which, or of any part of which, any conviction has been made under this Act, shall be held to be thereby confiscated, and the authority who has made the conviotion may make such disposal of them as he thinks fit. They may be kept for his own use, but shall not be sold or exported.
The provision in the last line, is, in my judgment, very objectionable. We had a case not long ago in which the officer who made the conviction kept the pelt of the animal, in respect to which the conviction was made, for his own use. Great fault was found, and it was thought that the effect of the punishment was very largely done away with by the fact that the convicting magistrate kept the pelt for his own use. I disapproved of it, but when I looked up the Act I found that it authorized the magistrate to do what he had done, and that the magistrate had only done what the Act permitted. All animals, birds, fish or eggs, or the pelt, skin or head of any animal, killed, trapped, snared or taken in violation of any provision of this Act, or any part of such animal, bird, fish, pelt, skin or head, shall, after the conviotion of the person who so killed, trapped, snared or took the same, respectively, be confiscated to the Crown by the authority who made the conviction

-who shall have power to declare the same so confiscated, and to order the sale or destruction thereof, and, If sold, the proceeds thereof shall be deposited and applied In the manner provided by section 15 of this Act; provided, that such convicting authority may give or direct any animal, bird, fish or egg so confiscated, or any part of such animal, fish or bird, to be given to any religious, charitable or scientific institution or purpose, as in his discretion seems proper.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the government to an article that appears in the Toronto News relative to the judiciary of Ontario. At the outset I may say that there are fifteen Superior Court judges in that province, and these are distributed in four different courts. We have first, the Court of Appeal composed of the chief justice and four puisne judges ; then the Chancery division with a chief justice and three iruisne judges; and then the King's Bench and Common Pleas divisions .similarly constituted. About eight months ago on the retirement of Sir George Burton, Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal, Justice Armour was promoted to the position and that left a vacancy in the King's Bench division. That vacancy has existed ever since. It is true that the government made an honest and strong effort to fill the vacancy, because it is well known that Mr. J. J. Foy, K.C., of Toronto, was proffered the position, but he for reasons best known to himself saw fit to decline. The fact that the vacancy has been allowed to exist for so long results in very great detriment and inconvenience to suitors. Under the procedure of our courts, on 891
action may be brought before one of the judges of the King's Bench division without a jury, and if one of the parties feels aggrieved by the judgment he may appeal, and his appeal will come in due course before that very same division. He has the adverse decision of the trial judge against him and his appeal comes before that very same judge again. Associated with the trial judge will be another justice of tfie court, and if the court divides in its opinion the appellant is left where he originally stood. If the vacancy were filled and there were three judges this could not occur. Again, there are certain actions in the High Court in which an appeal is not permitted to the court of appeal, If the litigant in such a case found himself with the two judges divided, and he then had the right to go to the court of appeal, his position would not be so bad, but he is debarred from going to the court of appeal and thus the unfortunate suitor lias to (face the judge who lias given an adverse decision against him. There was. for instance, what is known ns the West Durham case. In that case Chief Justice Falconbridge and Judge Street took different views, and the result was that the action was a nullity, and had to go to the Supreme Court. Had there been three judges in that court, two of them would of necessity have had the same opinion as against one, and that judgment might have been accepted and the case terminated. The Evening News says this, that the following notice has been posted at Osgoode Hall :
In consequence of it having become necessary for one of the judges to take the business assigned to the Hon. Mr. Justice Meredith, it has been found impracticable to continue the sittings of the divisional court this week.
If, however, there be any case of special urgency, a court may be specially constituted to hear it. Otherwise, no further sittings of the divisional court will. be held this month. By order of the court.
Fancy the position that these suitors are placed in. Take a case involving the ownership of a large quantity of saw-logs. It might be necessary at this time of the year to get these logs down the streams while the water is high, but owing to the fact that an injunction may be pending neither party can touch the logs, and great loss may result. This kind of thing will go on unless the government rises to the occasion. This government boasts that it is a strong government, and surely a strong government ought not be under the necessity of keeping a judgeship dangling before its friends in the province of Ontario for eight months. When the lamented death of Judge Rose caused a vacancy, an appointment was speedily made in the person of Mr. Justice Lount, and I may say that the appointment of that gentleman has given a very great deal of confidence to the bar of the province. But why this other vacancy

should be kept dangling for eight months it is hard to surmise. Had Mr. Foy accepted the position, he would have relieved the government from the trouble they find themselves in. I presume that the government has many applicants for the position, but I point out that it is humiliating to see what is going on in reference to this matter when it has been stated in the public press that petitions have been hawked about Toronto asking lawyers to sign them for the appointment of certain gentlemen to the bench.
That cannot do otherwise than bring the judiciary into disrepute, not only in the province of Ontario, but in other provinces as well ; for I have recently seen the statement in a Montreal paper that a judicial vacancy has existed in the province of Quebec for some time, and that a member of this House has threatened to resign if an appointment is made not to his liking. In view of the condition in which litigants find themselves in the province of Ontario, anld in view of the fact that the present condition of things is demoralizing to the opinion in which the judiciary is held by the public, I trust, now that the attention of the government has been called to the matter, that they waill announce that an appointment to the vacant position will speedily be made. I do not know who the fortunate gentleman may be. It is true, this government have evinced a disposition to confine the judicial appointments in the province of Ontario to their political friends. That was not always the case. The government of Sir John Macdonald appointed Mr. Samuel Blake and Mr. Justice Maclennan to the bench, and, I believe, the late Chief Justice Moss, a Liberal, was also appointed by a Conservative administration, though I am not sure as to that. In view of the statements which have been made in the press, and in view of the fact that the business of the courts is congested, I trust that the government will make an appointment to the vacant position at a very early day.

I have to express my regret that my hon. friend did not give me' any notice of' bis intention to bring this important question to the attention of the government. If I had been so notified, I would have informed myself as to the exact condition of judicial matters in the province of Ontario. I shall, therefore, have to answer only with such knowledge as I have. And at the outset I can say from the hon. gentleman's own statement, that I do not think the government are so guilty as he wants to represent them to be. My hon. friend, at the close of his remarks, said that this government had evinced a disposition to appoint to the bench only their political friends, whereas, in the earlier portion of his remarks. lie had stated, with equal emphasis, that this government had offered an appoint-

It is sent to public libraries, to mechanics' institutes, to the press, and to a number of other people. To send it to ail the schools would require an edition of 40,000 or 50,000, and a ten-fold increase of this voce.
Has the hon. gentleman reduced his staff in the Statistical Department ?
When I came into office in 1S90 there were a number of employees whom I dispensed with, but there has been no change within the last year or two.
That accounts for the delay in getting out the book.
I have not reduced the staff for the last three years. When I came into office those I dismissed were not engaged on the Statistical Year-Book, but on the remains of the former census.
What is the amount of the cost that would cover the cost of printing ?
Practically in this item, the whole amount. The salaries of the men who do the statistical work are in another item under civil government.

I agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram). I think it would be desirable that we should have a larger number Mr. FISHER.
of these books. It is a well prepared book, and it would be of infinite use in our schools. I know that in Montreal, very probably, you will not find in one of the elementary schools in that city, where they have 35,000 or 36,000 children, a single copy of the book. I think a great many of the pupils would be better employed perusing that book than many other books that they have in the schools. I think that next year the minister should make note of the necessity which exists throughout the country and make a larger distribution of that valuable volume.

I would like to give some figures which will show the hon. member for East Elgin that I am correct. In 1893 there were issued 3,374 copies of this book, 2,600 in English and 774 in French, at a cost of $4,43L In 1894 there were issued 2.400 copies in English and 750 copies in French ; that is to say, 200 less in English and 24 less in French than in the previous year, at a cost of $6,000 odd.
The book was larger ?

Yes, the book was larger. But, I may say that the book to-day contains all the information that it contained at that time in the way of statistical tables, and so on. By condensation and rearrangement the information is all there, although all the opinions that were expressed are not there. In 1895 there were issued 2,400 copies in English and 750 copies in French, at a cost of $6,000. In 1S96 3,000 copies in English and 1,000 copies in French were issued. It increased the first year that I came into office. The expense was only $2,100.
How was the reduction brought about ?

By condensing the book and doing the work more cheaply. In 1897 4,300 copies were issued in English and 1,200 in French. The edition of 5,500 cost $2,544. In 1898 the same number was issued, at a cost of $3,090. That was due to the increase in the wages of the Printing Bureau. In 1899 5,500 copies were issued, 4,300 in English and 1,200 in French, at a cost of $3,161.
Iloiy many copies does the hon. minister intend to issue this year-an increased number ?
If the cost per volume comes up to last year, I will have to continue with the same issue, because I have reached the limit of the money which I have at my disposal- $3,000.

The government have established a department of labour, and the duty of those engaged in this department

is to collect labour statistics. It strikes me that instead of creating another department, *when the department of statistics has been continued for years, if the government had employed such men as Mr. King and some parties to assist him, and allowed the department of statistics, as now conducted, to collect these labour statistics as well as other statistics, they would have been adopting a wise policy. It would save expense, and if members of parliament and others desiring information in respect to agriculture, labour, or any question affecting the welfare of the people, instead of getting the Statistical Year Book on the one hand, and taking a monthly pamphlet on the other, could get all these statistics in the Statistical Year Book, it would be much handier, because we could get all the information we required on any of these subjects in one volume. It would also be much cheaper than it is under the present system of having a statistical department controlled by Mr. Johnson, and a labour department controlled by Mr. King. I think the statistics would be more accurate, and they would be in a much more convenient form. There would also be the advantage otf being able to pro-cure the Statistical Year Book much quicker than it is issued to-day. As the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said, the great fault with the present Statistical Year Book is that too long a time is allowed to elapse between the end of the year with which the book treats, and the time when members of this House receive their copies. It is a great fault, because many persons, when they want to look up different questions, instead of referring to the Year Book, have to take the departmental reports to acquire the information that they desire.

I am not going into the general question of policy as to the Labour Bureau and the compilation of statistics. I do not agre'e with the hon. member for East Elgin, that, on the whole, it would be more handy for the public to have all these different kinds of statistics in the same volume. There are many people who want labour statistics, and who are not interested in the other statistics contained in this volume. There are those who are engaged in studying agricultural statistics who are not desirous of studying labour statistics.
Why not ?

Because they do not happen to be interested in those lines. They may not be or they may be. But they can get full information when the books containing all these particular things are issued. If you were to put all the statistics in one volume it would make a larger and bulkier volume, and those who do not wish to study one part would still have to take that part. The
hon. gentleman has to a considerable extent answered himself, when he said that the fault of the Statistical Year Book was, that the information did not come out until twelve or fifteen months from the end of the year for which it was compiled. In the Labour Gazette that information comes out month by month. The information is given promptly and accurately. The Labour Gazette is published for other purposes besides those of statistics, and it deals very largely with other things. I think it is better that all labour matters should be dealt with by men who are specially charged with that kind of work, and that statistical work of another 'character should be in the hands of others who are accustomed to deal with it. As to the general policy as to the establishment of a Labour Bureau and the publication of labour statistics, I do not know that it is necessary to go into that.
Does the hon. gentleman pretend to say that because a man wishes to find statistics affecting labour he would not be interested in questions of agriculture ?
No, I do not say so.

The hon. gentleman could not say so in reason, because it is a well-known fact that all those interests are so closely associated with each other that it is an important question for all persons who wish to understand public questions. I believe that by an increase in the staff of the statistical department, instead of reducing the staff, the Statistical Year Book would be published sooner, and it would be of more advantage to the public.
It never has been.
That is no reason why it should not be.
No.

Because we know perfectly well that some years ago the Statistical Year Book was a very large book, twice as large as it is to-day, and if you increase the staff, which could be done at a very small cost, it would be a great convenience to the public.
It is not because of the lack of staff ; it is because it comes out after the other departmental reports.

[DOT] The minister will have to find some other explanation for the delay. Every one knows that the Year Book is a mere repetition of tables, and that for each year there has only to be another year added. The book should come out Immediately after the departmental reports, because the figures are all in shape for the statis-

tician to classify them. Surely the hon. gentleman will not plead that because the Year Booh was late in publication in the past, that he should continue what I consider the insane policy of having a Statistical Year Book a year behind the time. There is not so much work about this after all. Hon. gentlemen on the Treasury benches, when they were in opposition, were not reputed to be friendly to the Year Book. It was made the subject of annual attack, and whether the minister shared these views or not, his friends were so hostile to it that he can hardly be expected to have become friendly within a few yeai;s. This is a useful book, but it is only useful if it is properly issued and in time. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) should give some other reason for his pursuit of this snail policy in the publication of this Statistical Year Book. I think the House will justify the minister in an increased expenditure if he needs a larger staff in order that we may have this book published in proper time, when it can be of use.

What I have stated here is the reason that has been given to me by the statistician. I confess I have left the matter very largely in the hands of Mr. Johnson, a gentleman who was the statistician when I took office, who has been carrying on the work connected with this book ever since it was inaugurated, and who, I believe, is competent to carry it on. I have not given the matter my personal supervision, but I will be glad to tell Mr. Johnson of the remarks made here, and see if he can work out a scheme which will satisfy the hon. gentleman.
The minister knows that he is responsible, and that Mr. Johnson is in no sense responsible.
Certainly.
Has the minister no suggestion of his own to make, rather than merely to tell Mr. Johnson what has been said in this House ?
I will be very glad if I can hasten the publication of this book.

The hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) is rather off the mark in charging the delay to the statistical department. What departmental reports does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) refer to ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) knows that some of the blue-books were not put on the Table until May of last year, and the Statistical Year Book, which is made up from them, was out of the Printing Bureau before June 30 last year.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) is not well informed or he would know that this book is always a year after the departmental reports are made.
And the minister admits it.

What I said was : that the statistics of the year ending June 30, 1899, are made up in the Year Book which is issued in 1900. about twelve months after, and that is what the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) has stated.
That is not what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) stated, but that is exactly what we are all saying here.

The hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) is correct in stating that the departmental blue-books were laid upon the Table of the House in the month of May last year, and the Statistical Y'ear Book was issued in June.
Not for the same year.

Whose fault was it that the departmental reports were not down before ?
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Our Year Book is like the Newcastle horse, very hard to catch and very little worth when you do catch him. I do not care so much for the delay, but I do say that the make-up of the book and the information it contains is not what should be expected from the Year Book for the Dominion of Canada. I have been in the habit for a long number of years of getting the Year Book of New Zealand, which I will place on the Table for hon. gentlemen to examine, and they will see a Year Book that is worth looking at. Both in the printing and in the information it contains the Canadian Year Book, when we do get it, does not do justice to this great Dominion of Canada.

If the Minister of Agriculture will take the trouble to look at the New Zealand Year Book he will feel considerable humiliation at the Year Book published by his department. The preface for the New Zealand Year Book of 1900 is dated August. 1900. and it states that parts of the book have been issued already and circulated in England, as the statistics were being prepared. It is only sufficient to look at the New Zealand Year Book to see how far we are behind. I can readily understand

from the remarks of gentlemen who were in the House before the present government came into power, why the Canadian Year Book is thought so little of by the government. I appeal to the minister to get out his Year Book as quickly as possible, and if he wants the necessary money for that purpose, we will not refuse it.
Aid to agricultural societies, $7,000.
The minister might tell us how this money is expended.

It is expended in the North-west Territories entirely. The local territorial government are not able to encourage agriculture in those territories in the same way that the local governments do in the different provinces, and for many years the parliament of Canada has voted this sum, which is distributed among the agricultural societies of the North-west Territories in proportion to their membership. A return is made every year to the department of the number of members of the different societies.

I do not object at all to the item, but I think it would be just as well if the whole truth were told in the estimates. Then this item would read: Aid to agricultural societies in the North-west Territories. We have a great deal of complaint from that section of the country that the people there are getting nothing at all. and when we are giving them $7,000, and giving nothing to the other parts of the country, I think we should state the fact.
Might I ask the bon. gentleman why it is given to the Northwest Territories and to no other portion of the Dominion ?

Each province has the power of taxation and can do this work for itself; but the North-west Territories are not organized, and the Dominion government, which has to act for the Territories, does the work there.
Will the minister explain the difference between the item Statistical Year Book and the item General Statistics, or are they the same ?

The item Statistical Year Book is for the printing of the book, while the item General Statistics is for certain temporary clerks who are employed in the department, in collecting statistics and doing work almost entirely for the book ?
Will the hon. gentleman tell the committee who furnishes the information upon which this grant is made, that is, with regard to the number of members of each society, and so on ?
It is furnished through the Department of Agriculture of the Territories.

The hon. gentleman said that the cost of the Statistical Year Book in 1893 was $4,000, in 1894 $0,000, in 1895 $0,000, in 1890 $2,100, in 1897 $2,500, iu 1898 $3,000, and in 1899 $3,100; but when we take these two items together we find that this year it will cost $0,200.
The figures I gave the hon. gentleman were for the printing alone, and did not include this item of general statistics.
It is not fair to the committee to say that is what the book cost.
The hon. gentleman does not mean to misrepresent me. The item before me was for the printing of the book, not for the compilation, which is done by the clerks in the department.
We did not understand that.
I cannot help that.
The hon. gentleman was claiming credit for the reduction of the cost of the book. Why did he not say that that was for the printing of the book alone ? Were these items always separate before?
Yes, always. The figures I read were a fair comparison with the cost in previous years.
Would the hon. gentleman say what both items amount to from 1893 to 1899 ?
I would have to look back at the estimates of previous years. The item of $3,200 has 1 believe been the same ever since I have been in office.
How many clerks are employed in this compilation, which costs $3,200 ?

They are as follows : Mr. Watts, $730; Mr. Munro, $725; Miss Ross, $672; Mr. Lepage, $050; sundry accounts, $423; making up the $3,200. But this does not include Mr. George Johnson's salary, nor the salaries of a couple of other clerks in the office.
The hon. gentleman unwittingly, I think, did mislead the committee. I was impressed with the remarks the hon. gentleman made. He was discussing the compilation as well as the printing.
No.
My hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) asked how the cost came to be reduced. The hon. gentleman's answer was that he had dismissed a staff,
wlio were at work on the census instead of [DOT]compiling this book, and there was a reduction in consequence.
No. no.
Is that money for agricultural societies paid to the North-west council, or to the individual societies ?
To the societies directly.
Upon a statement made by the North-west council ?

The statement comes through the Northwest council from the secretaries of the different societies, and is certified to as correct by the secretary of the Department of Agriculture of the North-west Territorial government, he getting the returns from the societies.

I am not going to quarrel with the grant, but I can say to the hon. gentleman that there is a great deal of slipshod business about it. There is a great deal of padding as to the number of members, which is without foundation, and I think it will be worth while for the hon. gentleman to make inquiry into the matter. He can see at a glance the opportunities there are, in the channels through which the information comes, without attempting to cast discredit on any one.

I may say that when I first came into office this grant was distributed without reference to the territorial government; and to avoid just what the gentleman suggests, and believing that the territorial government had more intimate relations with the people there, I required that the list of members should pass through their hands, thinking they could check it better than I could at this distance.
Experimental'farms, $80,000,

In view of the course taken by the Minister of the Interior with regard to the growth and planting of trees, and in view of what is being done in the experimental farms, the work of one department would seem to have run somewhat into the other. I think the hon. gentleman ought to state to the committee what is being done in that respect at the agricultural farm in Manitoba and the North-west Territories.

Ever since the establishment of the experimental farm, the attention of the staff has been turned to the cultivation of trees in order to find out what trees were most suitable for plantation in our territorial plains and then producing and distributing such trees as largely as possible to individual farmers. Mr. Mackay, the manager of the >t. CLANCY.
farm at Indian Head, started with sowing-seeds of certain kinds of trees, which Professor Saunders thought were likely to succeed. He also planted certain seedlings, some of which were procured from the adjoining northern states of the American union, some from Europe, and some from different parts of the Territories where tree seeds could be conveniently collected. This experimental work has been eminently successful. We have at Indian Head rows of trees which, I think, will average from 24 to 80 feet in height and which have beeu grown during the last twelve years, and today form most splendid wind-breaks. After careful investigation, we have found that for every foot added to the height of those wind-breaks, the effect upon the fields to the leeward has been extended forty to fifty feet. When a wind-break is ten feet high, it will help the culture of crops on a stretch of land about 500 feet out from the wind-break. When the tree is twenty feet high, it will affect an extent of 1,000 feet in width, and about forty or fifty feet more in width to every foot added to the height. This is of the utmost importance in those plains in which there has been found difficulty in raising successful crops in all seasons owing to the wind sweep. This work has been going on ever since the farm was started, and we have been able, by the distribution of small bundles of these young trees, to encourage the growing of trees in homesteads all over the North-west Territories. To-day there are many homesteads surrounded by little groves of trees, the first seedlings of which were sent out from the Brandon farm, which furnish striding object lessons to the people of the plains, and the result has been a constant stream of requests for these bundles of trees. But we could not possibly send out a very great number, and those we did send out were only sufficient to form object lessons, and not really form great stretches of wind-breaks for the practical working out of the problem of protecting our wind-swept plains. The Minister of the Interior appointed a gentleman some two years ago, Mr. See wart, to study this question of forestry, especially in the Territories, and Mr. Stewart came to the conclusion that it would be well for the Department of the Interior, which has ' charge especially of those lands, to largely increase the supply of such trees to the settlers. The officers of the experimental farm are entrusted with the duty of finding out wliat can be done, but it is not their duty to supply trees on a commercial scale or iu such numbers that the farmers can supply themselves with wind-breaks. That is a work which falls naturally on the Department of the Interior, in whose charge is the improvement and settlement of the public lands of the Dominion, and the officer in charge specially of this work has applied to me to allow the experimental farms to help him in producing large quantities of these

trees for general distribution. We have agreed to do this and have devoted a small portion of each of the farms at Brandon and Indian Head to the production of these trees. But as the experimental farms are intended for experimental work and not for commercial production of trees for the settlers, we have required that the Department of the Interior should pay to the Department of Agriculture the expenditure caused by this work, just as my department pays the Printing Bureau for the printing of the Statistical Year-Book, and the details are now being arranged between Professor Saunders and Mr. Stewart.

I understand from the hon. minister that the work carried on by the experimental farms is of an educational character, in order to ascertain the kinds of trees that will be suited to the country generally and to particular localities as well. That educational work must be to a very large extent already accomplished, and the remaining question is, how that western country can be supplied with proper wind breaks. Then it appears that Mr. Stewart was also called in by the Minister of the Interior to study the kind of trees best suited to that country.
I was impressed with what the hon. gentleman said had already been accomplished by the experimental farms. If the experimental farms have been engaged in carrying out this work, a useful work, I admit, to that country, there was no duty for Mr. Stewart to perform but to draw his salary-and that is what has been suspected from the first. I am afraid the hon. gentleman has given away the case of the Minister of the Interior. What the Minister of the Interior stated, and what Mr. Stewart stated, was, that the latter's efforts were directed toward finding what trees could be grown in that country. That work seems to have been performed by the experimental farm. If that is so, we had better do without Mr. Stewart ; or. if the experimental farms have been idle all this time in relation to work, we ought to know it. This matter was under the management of the former government. I am not going to say whether it was well or ill-conducted, but if it was not well carried out in the direction indicated by the hon. gentleman, it was useless then, and it is useless now. The hon. gentleman has said, as I understand, that the experimental farm expects to furnish tree plants for that whole country. But, the people of Canada hold that the government is not called upon to do more than carry on the educational work. There is no more reason why the government of Canada should furnish windbreaks at the public expense than there is why it should build barns for the farmers of that country. I am glad to hear the minister say that the educational work has been fairly well done in that country. And in the face of that statement the Minister
of the Interior should withdra w_ the grant that he has asked this House to give him for that purpose ; from the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture, it would seem that the department was teaching Mr. Stewart. I rather think the hon. gentleman is right in that. Because, as everybody knows, Mr. Stewart had not given this subject special study and was not specially informed upon it. He was respectably, and, I hope, profitably, employed for many years -all his life in fact-as a provincial land surveyor. He had nothing to do with matters of this kind, nor was he called upon to fit himself for a position of that kind. I am glad to have the hon. gentleman make the statement that the work is being well done by the experimental farms there, and after that statement, which I regard as very important, I think the House will hesitate to pay for the carrying out what I think I may characterize as the pretended work of Mr. Stewart.

It is not my duty, nor is it my purpose, to discuss the grant which has been made by this House, I believe, to my hon. friend, the Minister of the Interior, to carry out this work. But, I wish to say a word or two with regard to the sense in which the hon. gentleman has taken the question up. I am sure he does not wish in any way to misrepresent me. but he has tried to give a [DOT]complexion to what I said that is entirely different to what I intended. Mr. Stewart has not called in the officers of the experimental farm to teach him anything, but he is simply asking us to produce the plants which, according to his opinion from observation of the work on the plains will be useful for wind-breaks. Mr. Stewart's intention, as I understand from him-I was not present to hear the explanation that my hon. friend and colleague (Mr. Sifton) gave here the other night-is to give object lessons on a large scale to the people in the different parts of the plains, by planting wind-breaks on a considerable scale, perhaps half a mile or a mile long, for the purpose of showing the different kinds of trees that can be used-to carry on on a large scale the work that the experimental farm has been carrying on on an experimental scale.

The hon. gentleman will pardon me, but he was not present when the Minister of the Interior explained the matter. If he will consult ' Hansard ' he will see that on the application of any person the Department of the Interior would take the work in hand for that person.

And they will show how this work ought to be done to be successful, having studied the conditions, the methods and the requirements. It is to help the settlers to accomplish work which is so much in the interest
:2843*

of the country there. This work the experimental farm has not undertaken to do, because it was out of the line carried on at-the farm and by the officers of the farm. I have explained wliat the farms are doing, and I will leave the explanation of the other work to my hon. friend (Mr. Sifton), who is in charge of it.

I think the hon. minister stated that the work done by Mr. Stewart and the officers there is merely experimental.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE, I did not intend to say that. But, what I intended to say, and what I think I said, was that that was the work that the farm was doing.

Mr. Stewart stated that on the application of anybody, a man was sent out to give instructions as to tree planting. He views the land and makes a rough sketch, which is sent to the head office, where a plan Is drawn to a scale, and this officer will go back and see to the -planting of the wind-breaks. If that is to be done throughout Manitoba and the North-west Territories, the government will have a whole army of officers. I do not think that that should be done, nor do the members of this House, I believe. I should like to have an explanation as to the proportion of this $80,000 that is to go to each of the farms. Then, as to the course in giving out trees, have they given out small trees, or have they furnished the farmer with seeds ? I understand Mr. Stewart to say that where seeds could be given, it was better than to have the small trees planted.

The only place to which the Experimental Farm sent out trees to any extent is in the North-west Territories. Occasionally a few ornamental shrubs which we want to test are sent into eastern parts of the country, but that is not the regular work of the farm. In the North-west Territories, however, small bundles of perhaps a. dozen trees, or twenty or twenty-five in some dn-stances, have been sent up, young trees. In other cases small bags of tree seed have been sent out. The farm at Indian Head and at Brandon collect seeds from all the trees growing there every season, and these seeds are distributed when asked for, much in the same way that grain and potato seed are distributed from the other farms to the farmers for trial. The hon. gentleman asked what proportion of this amount was spent on the various farms. The Central Farm at Ottawa takes $42,000; that includes the salaries of the officers at the Central Farm, and I may say it also includes practically the whole of the seed distribution which goes on from the Experimental Farm.
Is the seed gathered on the farms in the North-west and British Columbia, distributed to the farmers there?

A part of it is, and a part of it is sent down here to be used in the eastern part of the Dominion. There is much more seed distribution proportionately from the Central Farm than from any branch farm. The maritime province farm takes about $9,000; the Manitoba farm takes about $10,000 ; the Indian Head farm about $10,000, and the British Columbia farm about $9,000.
Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture could tell what kind of trees have been found to be successful.

I could not say definitely without looking at the report, but I may say in a general way that the Manitoba maple has been found most successful, and is most generally used. There is also a tree called, I think, the Russian poplar that has been successfully used, but it breaks more easily than the Manitoba maple.
Has that been found successful all over the Territories ?

I could not say as to that. There are some parts in which it has been difficult to get any trees to grow successfully, but I think those parts are narrowing down. I think that in those sections where trees have not been grown successfully it has been owing to want of careful cultivation. I do not think the experiments of the Central Farm have yet shown a state of affairs about which we could dogmatize. It is possible that in certain sections other trees might be found more successful, because, although we have sent small packages of trees to the farmers in many parts of the Territories, I am sorry to say that in many cases the trees when planted have not been properly taken care of and treated as the directions called for. But we are not prepared to say that, because a package of trees sent to a particular farmer in a particular locality has not been successful in his hands, that therefore, they could not be successful elsewhere. But we take the reports as we get them and tabulate them as well as we can, and draw from them such conclusions as we feel justified in doing.

I can understand that there may be cases where the trees have not been given a fair chance ; but this work has been going on for many years, and surely the hon. gentleman will not now confess that he is unable to present any definite information as to the result of the experiments. I want to call his attention to a statement that was made in this House by a gentleman from the North-west to the effect that this Manitoba maple is the victim

of an insect, anil Inis been found a failure. That statement has been made in the House, I do not know whether the minister heard it; but the bon. gentleman who made that statement is sitting' in his place to-night. And he has stated that this tree of which the minister speaks has been planted In the vicinity of Winnipeg as well as in the Territories, and has been found to be a failure.
I would not undertake to give information on that point without looking into the matter more carefully.	_

Surely after the hon. gentleman painted in the most roseate hues the success of the Experimental Farm in tree planting, he is not now going to collapse and to say that he does not know anything about it.

This brings into question the position of Mr. Stewart. When I heard the description given by the Minister of Agriculture of the success of the experiments made in the North-west in regard to trees, and particularly trees planted as wind-breaks, it seemed to me, in the first place, that we must be ready to vote any amount of money to the experimental farms, and in the next place, I asked myself what the position of Mr. Stewart really was. Would the minister tell us what is the function of Mr. Stewart ? At one moment lie says that Mr. Stewart is working in conjunction with the employees of the farm in the North-west on extensive trials of tree planting for wind-breaks ; at another moment the minister disclaims any knowledge of Mr. Stewart, and the amount which we voted the other night he says he is not called upon to defend. Now, I would like to know what Mr. Stewart's position is there. Has he really under his direction a certain number of farm hands engaged in new experiments, experiments on a grand scale of planting wind-breaks half a mile long ? They say that he is not in the department of the minister. But, I find an immense variance between what the lion. Minister of the Interior told us as to the mission of Mr. Stewart in the North-west Territories, and that mission as explained to us by the lion. Minister of Agriculture. 1 would like to find some way of conciliating these two gentlemen before we proceed to adopt this resolution.

My hon. friend need not find any trouble. There is no difficulty in conciliating us. Mr. Stewart is an officer of the hon. Minister of [DOT] the Interior, and I have no details as to his work. Mr. Stewart does not report to me, and although I have talked with Mr. Stewart frequently, I have no information under my hand to give to fhe committee in regard to Mr. Stewart-
All I said about Mr. Stewart in connection with the experimental farms was, that by an arrangement between myself and imy colleague, the hon. Minister of the Interior, the director of the experimental farms is going to raise trees on the experimental farms for Mr. Stewart's work. I did not inquire particularly what Mr. Stewart is going to do with them. I have no control over Mr. Stewart's operations after he gets these trees, but that work is going to be carried out on the experimental farms at the expense of the Department of the Interior. I nave no further information in regard to Mr. Stewart's work to give to the committee on this occasion, and the vote which we are now discussing is not a vote for Mr. Stewart or a vote under the control of the department for which Mr. Stewart works.

That is about as clear as mud to me, because the hon. gentleman told us a moment ago that the work of his-departmeut in the North-west Territories was purely experimental. I understood him to say distinctly that the experiment in regard to raising trees had extended over several years and that the conclusion was arrived at that it was perfectly successful. Now, he tells us that the experimental farm is, under the direction of this officer, Mr. Stewart, to raise trees for experimental purposes.
The work is not going to be done under the direction of Mr. Stewart, but und^r the direction of the director of the experimental farms.
For Mr. Stewart.
All the trees that are produced are to be handed over to Mr. Stewart for his work.
For distribution.
For his work, whatever it may be.
Well, I give it up.
Hear, hear.
Perhaps the hon. minister could tell us the number of farmers to whom trees or tree seeds have been distributed from the different experimental farms. I presume he keeps a record of that.
Yes, there is a record, but I have not it under my hand. I could not give the hon. gentleman the number of farmers to whom tree seeds have been distributed.
For the past year ?
I do not see any record of it in the report of the Brandon farm.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if there is any truth in the alleged

statement of Mr. Stewart which was repeated here the other night that all experiments in tree planting in the North-west Territories had utterly failed and that Mr. Stewart's mission was to go around preaching the proper doctrine of tree planting, and to give the people instruction as to how trees could he raised and proper experiments could be made. That statement was made here, and I would ask the hon. minister how he reconciles it with his own splendid experiments in the North-west ?
I do not attempt to reconcile it. I do not know whether it was made or not.

The hon. gentleman stated in the early part of the evening that it was found to be difficult for the agricultural farms to produce trees to any considerable extent for planting in the country more than merely for experimental purposes. I understood the hon. gentleman to make that statement.
I said we had not done so before.
Am I to understand that the hon. gentleman intends to enlarge the building of tree planting now ?

Yes, at these farms for this purpose.
_ Mr. CLANCY. Does the hon. gentleman intend to grow trees at the experimental farms*to provide wind-breaks in the country ?
I propose to raise trees and to hand them over to Mr. Stewart for whatever uses his department requires them and Mr. Stewart's department, the Department of the Interior, has to pay for that work.
But, it is paid out of the public purse.
Yes.

What I ask the hon. gentleman is if he is going to devote, to" a larger extent than in the past, tile efforts of the farms to the growth of trees for the purpose of making wind-breaks upon the application of such parties as may apply to the Department of the Interior, 'is his department to be a pack horse for the Department of the Interior ? The hon. gentleman stated in most explicit terms, that, while in the past, only a comparatively few trees were grown for educational purposes, now he intends to enlarge the service and hand the trees over to Mr. Stewart to make windbreaks in the country. I do not think I am misstating the hon. gentleman in the statement that I make. If It is the intention for the Agriculture Department to furnish trees to the Department of the Interior because the Department of the In-1 Mr. MONK.
terior pays for them it is a mere change of tyrants. It does not make any difference which pays for them; it all comes out of the public purse. The question is : Should it be paid for at all in the sense of work that is to be carried out by Mr. Stewart ?
That is another matter.
In the distribution of these trees to the farmers, are they to be charged for, or are the farmers to pay anything for them ?
My department has nothing to do with the distribution of them. We hand them over to Mr. Stewart's branch and he deals with them entirely.

In connection with that, we would require more information because you are establishing a new line. It is practically the establishment of nurseries for the benefit of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. If you are going to supply the demand for trees which will be enormous in the future it would be well for us to know whether they are to be supplied free or to be charged for. If you are to become the patrons of the farmers in the whole country it would be a very expensive business.

I am not going to give them to the farmers. I am going to give them to the Department of the Interior and I am not able to give the hon. gentleman any information. The information does not really affect this vote because the money asked for here is not going to be used for that purpose in any way whatever. I do not raise any technical objection to the hon. gentleman's questions; I would be glad to give him the information if I could. But, the work, being paid for by the Department of the Interior, I am not in a position to give him any information in respect to it. This work is not being done by my officer, but by an officer responsible to and paid by that department. The products will be handed over to them to do with them as they see fit according to the needs of their work. I am not responsible for that part of it.

This vote in the first instance applies directly to the experimental farms. They are undertaking a new line of work for which the hon. Minister of Agriculture asks an amount to be voted in the estimates.
No, Sir.

Well now, will the hon. minister wait till he hears the statement I am about to make before he so emphatically contradicts it ? I say that he asks for that item in the estimates for these experimental farms while at the same time he tells us

that they are undertaking this work. It is for us to say whether it is the part of wisdom to commence this divergence or not. Therefore, it is necessary to get this information to enable us to judge whether it is wise to keep up the farms for that purpose. I think the hon. minister ought to be in a position to give that information to the committee.

No increased expenditure which is required for this work is to be taken out of the vote under consideration. The land of the farm is to be used, it is true, but any other work in connection with the raising of these trees for this purpose is to be paid for by the Interior Department.

Perhaps only a dozen farmers may apply this year, but if the experiment is a great success there may be a thousand applications next year. This will, of course, entail increased work on the farms, and before we determine whether it is wise to maintain these experimental farms for that purpose, we should have the information I have asked for.
I cannot give any more information.

I do not think that is at all fair. As the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) has pointed out, we are embarking upon a new policy. I am far from saying that it is not a proper thing to maintain these tree nurseries for the farmers of the North-west, but surely we are entitled to know what amount out of this vote is to be expended for the cultivation of these trees.
No portion of this vote will be so expended.
Who will pay the expense then ?

The Minister of the Interior will pay the expense in that connection. I have already explained that no part of this $80,000 will be devoted to that work. The farm work will be carried on as it has been in the past, and every bit of work connected with the raising of these trees will be paid for out of the Interior vote.

Then, we are commencing to divide the farm work between two departments of the government, and that is a bad system. In the past we thought it wise to keep all this work under the Department of Agriculture, so that we might see at a glance what is the expenditure and what is the progress made. If the Department of the Interior becomes a co-partner with that of Agriculture, it will be more complex and more difficult to get at the value of the work done.

Although the work is going to be paid for by the Department of the Interior, that 90
department will not have anything to do with the actual management of the work. The work will be done by the farm at the expense of the Interior Department, but it will be done by my officers and by the hands employed on the farm, and if more hands are needed, as they will be for this work, the time and the work of those hands will be charged to the Minister of the Interior, just the same as the Printing Bureau charges my department with printing other work.

Suppose that on one of these farms a dozen men are employed and three are engaged in the arboretum, and the demand will so increase in the future that it will require a couple of hundred hands to supply it, that extra demand would not be in connection with the farm work, and yet we will be called upon to vote larger sums year after year, to meet this increased employment of labour.
Through the Department of the Interior.
Will not the Department of Agriculture pay for the farm hands ?
It is impossible for me to explain any further than I have.

The minister told us a few minutes ago that this vote covered the salaries of the farm hands. But suppose this work requires a far greater number of hands, will we not be obliged to vote a larger sum year after year to pay them ? In order to enable us to determine if it is wise to enter into this business, it is essential that we should have the information that we ask. As soon as the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture get through their consultation, I will resume. I am not talking for the mere amusement of it, nor for the purpose of killing time, but with the endeavour-somewhat ineffectual, I admit- to get information which we ought to know before we can intelligently vote this money. We ought to know upon what line it is proposed to distribute these trees to the farmers, and whether or not, an unlimited number will be supplied in the future, as the demands may increase.

I must tell the hon. gentleman frankly that that is information which I cannot give. My hon. colleague (Hon. Mr. Sifton) has that information, and I believe gave it to the House when) he got the vote out of which this expenditure is paid. I have explained that the money which I am asking now will not go for that purpose, and therefore I do not chink I can fairly be called upon to give that information.

Do I understand that no portion of this $80,000 will be applied to the distribution of the trees ?

In answer to my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson), I wish to say that I have found a statement of the amount of tree seed, and trees distributed from the Brandon farm last year. Yes.
In the Auditor General's Report (D-31) there is an amount of $395.46 for distribution of trees from the Brandon Experimental Farm. Do these trees go to farmers in that neighbourhood ?

That is a detail of the work as to which I am not in a position to give information to the committee, because it belongs to my colleague's department. While I have talked the matter over with him, I have not under my hand the details as to how the work is to be done.

When we come to Mr. Stewart's mission in the North-west, the Minister of Agriculture reminds me of a character in one of Dicken's novels, who, whenever asked a question, replied : * You must really know what you want to know.' standing with the Department of the Interior as to the extent to which this treeplanting would be carried as an experiment in favour of the farmers of the North-west. It looks like a vote of want of confidence in the Minister of Agriculture by the Minister of the Interior. Now the work is to be taken out of his hands by the Minister of the Interior. The hon. gentleman's department will do the menial work of planting seeds, but as soon as the trees are above the ground the Minister of the Interior will take charge of them and will become the medium between the farm and the farmers. Would the minister tell us about the number of stock on these farms, and what experiments are being carried on generally ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULi l. RE. The annual report of the farms gives full details of the number of head of animals of all kinds on each farm. I could look up the report, and give it to the committee if

the hon. gentleman insists upon it; but I do not think that is what .he means. We hare on these farms cattle, sheep, swine anil poultry as well as horses for the carrying-on of the work. In round figures we have at. the present time on the experimental farm at Ottawa 125 or 130 head of cattle, 35 or 40 sheep, 40 or 50 pigs, and between 100 and 200 head of poultry. I would not like to give a more exact statement without referring to the actual figures. At the farm of the maritime provinces at Nappan we have probably 75 head of cattle, including the young calves, 40 or 50 pigs, 30 or 40 sheep, 40 or 50 head of poultry, and the horses necessary for carrying on the work. We have at Brandon about the same number as at Nappan, and at Indian Head, about the same-perhaps not as many cattle. I do not think we have any sheep at either Brandon or Indian Head. At Agassiz, B.C., we have a smaller stock-20 or 25 head of cattle, 12 or 15 sheep, 20 or 30 pigs, some poultry and a few horses. The hon. gentleman has asked me about the lines of stock breeding and general work. I must be pretty general. The details of all this are given before the Committee on Agriculture every year by the officers of the farm, and it would be tedious and, I think, unimportant for me to go into the details. But generally I may say that at the farm here and at the Nappan, farm we carry on considerable dairy work, besides feeding cattle for beef every winter. I have a number of steers fattened every spring, most of which were bought in the fall and sold in the spring. They are fed on experimental lines, and the results are published in the report for the information of all those interested in feeding stock. The feeding of swine and sheep and poultry is also carried on for the same purpose. The farms in the west are less devoted to dairying, although at each some cows are kept all the year round.

A few years ago there was considerable tuberculosis among the stock, and while a number were slaughtered, I understood that some were kept in quarantine under treatment. What has been the result of that treatment ?

There was none of that stock kept at the farm. The animals that were found to be tuberculous were slaughtered, with the exception of ten head, which were sent to Montreal, and put into a small quarantine station to be treated by Dr. McEachran. They were kept about ten months and then slaughtered. Since that other animals have been quarantined in the same way. and subjected to various experiments, but there have been no tuberculous animals on the farm since the spring or winter of 1897. Since then we have carefully tested every animal purchased with the tuberculin#, and when, as has occurred in very few instances, 904
reaction took place, the animal was>
slaughtered immediately.
Has the hon. gentleman made up his mind as to the value of the tuberculine test ?
That subject will be more properly treated under the heading of the tuberculosis vote.

No, because that matter is now being ar- ' ranged between Prof. iSaundei-s and Mr. Stewart, and the details are not yet settled.

$1,500 will cover the expense.
Then, it is evident not much will be done.

speechtext: Certainly $1,500 is not going to meet the expense of raising and distributing these trees and supplying all the tools necessary to cultivate them. If the Department of the Interior is to run the business, why not give the land to that department, and not make a joint account ?
Because it is considered that the work will be done more cheaply and better by the experimental farms.
Have any representations been made to the hon. minister for the establishment of a farm-I do not say an experimental farm-but a farm under government control in the province of Quebec ?

Requests have come from various parts to increase the number of experimental farms. The Experimental Farm Act specifies the number and where they shall be. The farm at Ottawa is on the boundary between Quebec and Ontario, so that it serves these two great provinces. That was the decision arrived at by our predecessors, whom the hon. gentleman and his friends have supported.
I confess that I consider that the number of experimental farms at present is sufficient for the needs of the experimental work of the country, so far as great experimental farms can carry on that work. I have always believed as I stated when the establishment of the experimental farms was originally proposed, that it would have been better if, instead of the great farms, farms smaller in extent and less expensive in their management-small illustration or experimental stations-had been established all over the country. That view was not accepted at the time. Great establishments were made at the various points, and a large amount of money was spent on them, and a large amount of annual expenditure entailed. We would not be able to change that whole policy without making a radical change in the Act, and involving the country in large additional expenditure. The work has been done on the lines laid down, it has been carried out by the officers in an excellent manner. I am glad to say that this work inaugurated by my predecessors in office and my political opponents has been well carried out, and has resulted in great advantage to the farming industry and population of the country. I am not prepared, in view of the large expenditure of the farms to-day, to propose a radical change in the farm policy. I have had it in view, as is well known to hon. members who were in the last parliament to extend the work with establishments on a smaller scale. But that was met with such opposition by hon. gentlemen opposite, and by other gentlemen in this House, that it was dropped. I still believe that it would be in the interest of agriculture and of the community at large, if such a change could be brought about. But I have not seen my way to repeat the proposal this session. It would not have involved any change in the management or equipment of the present experimental farms.

The hon. gentleman has gone far beyond the question I asked him. What I wished to elicit a reply to is this-as he says there is no desire in the province of Quebec to have a complete experimental farm ; but representations have been made, I believe, and figures laid before him to show that the Experimental Farm at Ottawa is not easily accessible, and therefore it is desired that a station upon a modest scale, a sort of model farm, should be

established near Montreal. I wished to know if the minister had arrived at a decision on these representations. I know that such representations have been made from my own county.
Similar representations have been made from various sections all over the country.

I am going to answer the hon. gentleman's question, but in the way I think right to answer it. Similar representations and requests have been made from various parts of the country, from Vancouver on the west to Prince Edward Island on the east.
