I would point out, in the first place, that what we may call agricultural education, like every other kind of education, is purely within the sphere of the provincial government, and the provincial law. Several of the provinces of the Dominion have provided out of their own resources for the agricultural education within their boundaries, which I think is the proper method of providing for education, agricultural or otherwise.
There they are trying to settle them on lands owned by themselves, but the Dominion own the lands in Manitoba and the North-west Territories with regard to settlement.

I wish to point out that the work of the experimental farm is not in any way connected with teaching people on those farms to do farm work. The experimental farms are for the purpose of investigating facts and truths in connection with the production and utilization of farm crops. That
experimental work is entirely inconsistent with the teaching of ignorant pupils. That must be done by those who have a scientific training. I venture to think that such a system in the experimental farm would involve a radical change in the whole aim and object of those farms, and would be entirely inconsistent with their present work.
Is any portion of this vote used for repairs of buildings at the farms ?

It is used for the purchase of implements, but not for repairs of buildings, which are done by the Public Works Department.
Printing and distribution of reports and bulletins of farms, $4,000.

Fumigating stations, $2,500.

This is for fumigating the nursery stock imported under the amendment to the San Jos6 Scale Act. At first we prohibited the importation, but we afterwards discovered that it was possible to fumigate the stock so as to completely destroy the scale; We agreed to establish fumigating stations at different ports, similar to the cattle quarantine stations. These stations are : St. John, N.B. ; St. Johns, P.Q. ; Niagara Falls and Windsor, Ont. ; Winnipeg, Man. ; and Vancouver, B.C. We require to appoint, for a short time in the spring and fall of the year, a man to do the fumigating work.
I asked the minister, before we reached this item, if he could give us any information as to what success attended the effort to stamp out the San Josd scale.

My department is not undertaking to stamp out the scale, except in so far as the entomologist and botanist of the Experimental Farm are giving information by letter, and word of mouth, and visit to any one who asks for information regarding the pest. We are taking no active steps towards stamping it out in the sense that the Ontario government has been taking steps. The San Jose scale exists in Canada only in the province of Ontario, I think. I am not speaking from my own personal knowledge, but from the reports in the newspapers and the debates in the Ontario House, and the statements that are made at public meetings. These sources of information are as available to the hon. gentleman as they are to me, and, perhaps, I may not be correct in every detail as to what I am saying. The Ontario government have been taking active steps in trying to stamp out the scale, and if they cannot stamp it out, to prevent its being spread. One of the most effective steps which I think they have successfully taken has been to require that all nursery stock raised in the province should be fumigated before being distributed by the nursery men. I believe that the nursery men are fumigating the stock, and if they do that there is, I think, not the slightest danger of the spread of the San Jos6 scale from that source. Our work has been directed entirely to protecting this country from the importation of this scale from abroad. We first of all prohibited the importation of nursery stock altogether, but we afterwards amended the Act so as to allow the importation. under certain conditions, which. I believe, will prevent any danger of the importation of the scale. The work has been carried on last fall and last spring, and it has been done thoroughly and satisfactory.

The scale is a thing which spreads from tree to tree and from farm to farm. I am not aware that it has been spreading - to new sections of the country, although I understand that it has been spreading over a slightly greater area in the province of Ontario than it was before. I think, too, it has been found in some parts where it was not believed to be before; but it was found on old trees, and not on nursery stock. The statement that fumigation is ineffectual is entirely unfounded. On the contrary, we have had no reports of any eases from nursery stock which has come into the country and has been fumigated at ' those stations; and as the matter is largely in the minds of the horticulturists and tree-growers, I am sure the fact would have been reported to us had the scale been so found.

The hon. gentleman attributed to me a statement which I did not make. I asked if the fumigation was effectual, or could it be that the scale was spread through that means ? I noticed a report last fall that while the scale was at first thought to be confined to a limited area in the Niagara district, it was afterwards found in different districts between Niagara and the Western Peninsula, and that it was believed to be spreading with

considerable rapidity. I also saw in the same communication that the Department of Agriculture had abandoned the idea of eradicating the scale from the country. .	,
You have reference to the Department of Agriculture for Ontario, not to this department.
I understood it applied both to the Department of Agriculture of Ontario and the department here as well.
No.
The first proposal was, of course, to destroy the trees on which the scale was found and to fumigate the stock. 1 understood that that first plan was abandoned.
All the work the hon. gentleman is discussing was the work of the department at Toronto, not of this department at all.
This department outlined the methods by which it was thought it could be eradicated, and it was proposed to take up the work jointly with the Department of Agriculture for Ontario.
No.

The hon. gentleman says no, but I remember the discussion distinctly. The question was asked, why keep it out if there is no effort to stop it in the country, and the answer was that the Department of Agriculture lor Ontario would endeavour to destroy it in the country, and the effort of this department would be directed to prevent its importation, and by these joint means we would hope to get rid of it. It is quite clear that one or both were out in their judgment, and that the means adopted were not as effectual as it whs thought at that time they would be. It may be that we are preventing the importation of it, and yet it may be found after a while that we are not.
Tracadie Lazaretto, $5,500.

Last year, the hon. minister will remember, I brought up the case of the Chinese lepers in British Columbia. I pointed out to him how manifestly unfair it was that the government had not taken charge of those lepers. At the present time and for many years past the cities of Victoria and Vancouver have had to pay for the maintenance of those lepers. Large sums of money are collected every year from the Chinese who land in British Columbia, as head tax-over $200,000, the larger proportion of which goes into the Dominion treasury. care of them, because they had agreed to do so when New Brunswick entered confederation. That is not an accurate statement of fact.

Well, they have not paid anything for the last two or three years. What is the reason British Columbia cannot expect the same treatment from the government as Nova Scotia and Manitoba ? There is not a man in British Columbia but thinks the same as I do with regard to that matter-that it is unfair to make flesh of one and fish of another. I cannot understand it unless it is because Victoria has always sent Conservatives here to represent it. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman on what ground he has refused persistently to maintain these lepers in British Columbia ?

I stated a few moments ago that the hon. gentleman's statement was not accurate. I understood him to lead the House to believe that the Conservative government had paid $1,000 a year for several years.
So they did.
The hon. gentleman is incorrect. They paid it one year. They did not pay it the year before I came into office, and it has not been paid since.
They paid it more than one year.

The hon. gentleman says so; I say they did not. It was open for discussion at the time, and I looked into the matter and decided it was not necessary or proper that the department should pay, and I declined to pay it.

Because it was a matter affecting the public

health of British Columbia, with which the people of British Columbia should deal.

Because the lepers in Manitoba were immigrants who had come in through the departmental work of this government, and therefore this government was responsible for their presence in the country.

to go through these institutions as I have done and study the records.
